name: Ecuador
summary_text: Ecuador demands real caution from trans visitors — a country whose legal framework is now among Latin America's strongest while its streets are among the region's most dangerous. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016; the 2024 Organic Law reform lets adults change name and sex/gender on the ID card directly through the Civil Registry (one time, no surgery); and in 2024-25 Constitutional Court rulings extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the Assembly for stalling trans-rights implementation. The violence side is severe: Runa Sipiy documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023, with inadequate state response, and the “internal armed conflict” against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024 — two more LGBTQ people killed in its first weeks. Quito and Guayaquil carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis. For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in South America right now.

sources.claim_summary: AP (Spanish): 'Ecuadorians can now change sex in addition to gender on identity documents' — the LGBTI+ community welcomes a legislative reform allowing the sex marker on IDs to be amended, reducing registry barriers.

sources.title: Presidente Noboa emite reglamento para ley que viabiliza cambio de sexo o género en cédula de identidad
sources.claim_summary: Primicias (June 2024, in Spanish): President Noboa issued the regulation implementing reforms to the Identity Management and Civil Data Law, allowing people to rectify the sex field or replace it with gender on national ID cards (cédula) via the Civil Registry.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Los Angeles Blade piece (Jan 2024) reports violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians increasing amid the internal armed conflict.
AP (Apr 2026): 'A transgender teen's case in Ecuador opens path for others seeking legal recognition' — Constitutional Court rulings let trans adolescents change name and sex on official records.

sources.title: Ecuador | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex marriage legal since 2019 (adoption still barred by constitutional ban); legal gender recognition since 2016 but not available under 18; conversion practices partially prohibited, with torture-based conversion explicitly criminalised; constitution bans discrimination on sexual orientation but gender identity/expression/sex characteristics not explicit; police and prosecutors often fail to investigate hate crimes.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Ecuador: documents discrimination based on sexual orientation among societal problems, alongside excessive police force, media restrictions and corruption - baseline context.

Georgetown Political Database of the Americas: English text of Ecuador's 2008 Constitution - Article 11(2) prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the constitutional framework underpinning LGBT rights in Ecuador.

sources.title: Gay family recognised by state in Ecuador in historic decision | PinkNews
sources.claim_summary: PinkNews (May 2018): Ecuador's Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register a 7-year-old girl with both mothers' surnames - a historic recognition of LGBT families; context: decriminalisation 1997, civil unions 2015, and a 2016 law allowing people to choose their preferred gender on ID cards; adoption and surrogacy gaps remain.
